questions.question: Name three key discoveries in the control of disease and explain how each lowered death rates.
questions.expected_answer: Jenner's smallpox vaccine (1796) prevented smallpox, later eradicated (1980); Pasteur's germ theory (1860s) showed germs cause disease, leading to hygiene, pasteurisation and antiseptics; Lister's antiseptics (1867) cut deaths after surgery; Fleming's penicillin (1928, mass-produced 1940s) cured bacterial infections such as pneumonia and infected wounds; later vaccines (polio, measles) prevented child deaths.

questions.question: Explain how John Snow's work and improved sanitation reduced deaths in nineteenth-century cities.
questions.expected_answer: In 1854 Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho, London, and found they clustered around the Broad Street pump; removing its handle reduced cases, showing cholera spread through contaminated water, not bad air. After the Great Stink of 1858, London built sewers (Bazalgette) to carry waste away from drinking water; cities built piped clean water, water treatment and rubbish collection, sharply reducing cholera, typhoid and dysentery deaths.

questions.question: How did canned food and refrigeration affect health and population?
questions.expected_answer: Canning (Appert 1810, tin cans) and refrigeration (refrigerated ships from the 1870s-80s, home fridges in the 20th century) preserved food safely by killing or slowing germs, allowing storage and long-distance transport. This improved nutrition and food security, reduced illness from spoiled food and scurvy, made people more resistant to infection, and so lowered death rates; refrigeration also keeps vaccines effective (the cold chain).
